title: Legal AI, Trust, and Agents: Joel Hron on Thomson Reuters, Anthropic, and the Future of CoCounsel
author: Joel Hron

kp.k: Claude's legal expansion changes competition without replacing enterprise platforms
kp.d: Stephanie Wilkins reports that Anthropic announced 12 practice-area plugins, more than 20 MCP connectors with legal-tech providers, Microsoft 365 expansion, access-to-justice partnerships and a managed-agents layer. She characterises this as an inflection point rather than an overnight industry transformation. Reporting Legaltech Hub's analyses, she says research capabilities differ across BigLaw, small firms and solo access-to-justice practitioners, and enterprise platforms are not yet replaceable on a lift-and-shift basis; the transcript does not supply those analyses' underlying findings.
qs: The first one covers the full announcement, that there are 12 new practice area plugins, more than 20 MCP connectors with legal tech providers, expansion across Microsoft 365, access to justice partnerships, and a managed agents layer for legal users building in the Claude platform developer environment.
And then a fourth piece by Nikki Shaver really dives into the operational reasons why Claude for Legal is simply not yet a lift-and-shift replacement for enterprise legal AI platforms.
It has not upended the industry overnight, but there is a lot to follow here, and we’re going to keep looking at it from different angles as they arise.

kp.k: Professional accountability anchors Hron's fiduciary-grade AI strategy
kp.d: Hron defines Thomson Reuters' fiduciary-grade approach around professionals' continuing accountability and the transparency, auditability and verifiability needed to stand behind AI-assisted work. He reports recurring trust concerns during two weeks of customer discussions across corporations, Am Law 100 and global large firms, and major tax firms. These are vendor-reported customer conversations, not a quantified study or an independent professional standard.
qs: I think the core premise of this idea is that almost right is not good enough in the domains that we deal with.
I think the professional maintains that accountability.

And so it’s incumbent, I think, on us as software providers to build the tools in terms of verifiability and transparency and auditability to give them what they need in order to stand behind the output.

kp.k: Legal content and checking tools differentiate agent capabilities
kp.d: Hron says Thomson Reuters combines frontier models and agent harnesses with its legal content, citation-ledger tools and automated checking capabilities. He cites 1.9, almost 2 billion documents across Westlaw and Practical Law and 1.5 billion KeyCite validity signals as resources for extending lawyers' existing trust mechanisms to AI. He describes this architecture at a high level, without providing the patent-pending ledger architecture or an explicit open-web exclusion requested by the host.
qs: And I would say our focus has really been around how do we exploit the value of the 1.9, almost 2 billion documents across Westlaw and Practical Law that we have, the 1.5 billion KeyCite validity signals.
These are all signals that human lawyers use every day to validate and verify and build trust in the work product that they’re putting out to their clients or to the courts or otherwise.

And again, those tools lean on access to the content and information we have, but specifically also verification tools, citation ledger tools that we are able to build that allow the agent to do that work of verification for itself and ultimately deliver a better work product at the end of the day.

kp.k: Agents extend legal research into routine transactional tasks
kp.d: Hron describes the next CoCounsel version, then in beta, as applying the Deep Research approach across more legal tasks. He says the agent consults legal content on almost every task, including contract-clause modification and provision updates, to check current market practice and relevant case history. This is his account of product behaviour and potential content value, not a measured productivity result.
qs: And that next version of CoCounsel is in beta right now.
It does legal research on almost every task.
If it’s modifying a contract clause or updating terms in a provision or something like this, it is always doing research.

What you see is that these AI systems, when you give them these tools, are actually using this content in a really deep way across many different types of legal work that you might not have considered doing research for before.

kp.k: Claim-level analysis aims to reduce human verification burdens
kp.d: Responding to Lambert's report that lawyers can spend almost as much time checking AI answers as obtaining them, Hron describes Litigation Document Analyzer as decomposing documents into assertions and tabulating their legal support or lack of support, including possible overstatement of authorities. He asserts that this speeds human verification but provides no timing measurements. He explicitly treats the product as recognition that generated briefs and reports may never be completely accurate.
qs: And what this system will do is it’ll go through every claim made in this document.
The output of this is effectively a table of, here are all the claims, and here is the support or lack of support for this claim.
That absolutely speeds up verification.

I think, in fact, us building those products is recognition that it may never be 100% accurate, and lawyers need tools to be able to build trust in the work ultimately so that they can stand behind it and be accountable for it.

kp.k: MCP enables distribution beyond proprietary legal interfaces
kp.d: Hron positions CoCounsel as both a dedicated application and a legal-capability agent available within other systems, including general AI tools, workplace software and customers' own applications. He argues that MCP changes access rather than the underlying competitive advantage of trusted legal intelligence. His anticipated headless workflows can run automatically from an email and return results by email, while dedicated interfaces remain useful at important verification stages.
qs: The interface layer of software, as you guys have said, has been democratized quite a lot by AI tools, and in particular coding tools and things like that.
And we see a lot of firms building their own things.
MCP changes access, not advantage, if that makes sense.
It may be a workflow that gets triggered automatically off of an email, and a series of steps and work happens, and it comes back as another email.

Users can access that via MCP and plug it into different places, but CoCounsel, the UI, is our expression of that agent and how we believe a lawyer can get the most out of that agent for certain types of tasks.

kp.k: Interfaces increasingly support explanation and transfer of human context
kp.d: Hron says development increasingly starts with agent capabilities, with interface and agent teams jointly identifying gaps that can require better workflows, customisation, tools or behaviour. He frames legal interface design around explaining why claims are made and helping professionals communicate context the agent lacks, using onboarding an intern with shared documents as an analogy.
qs: I would say most of the development we do today really starts with the agent.
And I think as we build UIs that express those capabilities, those UIs convey obvious gaps.
how do I build a user experience that elicits that understanding of how and why this claim is made, rather than just surfacing the claim in pretty font and colors?
And in many ways, the UI itself is a way to help the human user convey their context to the agent in a way.

kp.k: Hron distinguishes instructional plugins from trusted legal systems
kp.d: Hron characterises Anthropic's standalone legal plugins as rudimentary instructions rather than systems providing validation, factual grounding or transparency. He argues that integrating CoCounsel through MCP could add those capabilities. His suggestion that Anthropic intends the plugins as illustrative starting points rather than comprehensive legal products is explicitly his interpretation, not a statement from Anthropic or a comparative performance evaluation.
qs: So I would say the plugins themselves have no concept of validation or verification or groundedness in factuality in any way.
Now that’s not to say that one couldn’t take a plugin and say, hey, use these tools to validate your work along the way.
And those tools could be CoCounsel MCP, living in a plugin.
I also don’t think Anthropic’s goal is to build a legal product per se that covers the spectrum.

kp.k: Secure, agent-accessible institutional knowledge becomes a competitive priority
kp.d: Hron identifies security and trust as barriers between AI capability and real-world use. He states that Thomson Reuters does not use the customer information under discussion to train its models and products. He recommends that firms and corporations invest in expertly codifying, owning and serving proprietary knowledge in agent-native forms, predicting competitive advantage for those doing this better than rivals rather than treating knowledge capture casually.
qs: And we’ve been very clear that we don’t use that information in terms of training our models and products and things like that.

In the future, if you can codify your knowledge, and we’ve talked about knowledge management as a domain of law for a while, but if you can codify your knowledge in a way, and you can do it better than the next person and make that knowledge available for AI in agent-native ways, then I think you have a tremendous competitive advantage.
Owning that knowledge is really what differentiates you at the end of the day as a company.

kp.k: Agent use requires redesigning underlying legal information infrastructure
kp.d: Hron compares Thomson Reuters' organisation of case law, statutes and regulations with firms organising accumulated matter experience to inform future work. He says the company has changed foundational aspects of Westlaw and supplies agents with different APIs from those powering the human-facing application because agents interact with content differently and at different speeds and rates.
qs: That is the same job that we do with case law and statutes and regulations.
We just happen to do it with most jurisdictions across the world.

we have changed the foundational aspects of how Westlaw works for agents versus how it used to work for humans, and the APIs that the agent calls are different than the APIs that power the application today because agents work with the content in a different way, at a different pace, and at a different rate than humans do.

kp.k: AI coding adoption offers an analogy for professional restructuring
kp.d: Hron reports an organisational objective that AI write more than 50% of codebase pull requests, with some teams above 80%. He uses 51% as a mental model for shifting engineers from writing code to constructing governance systems, tests, guidance and architectural constraints. He anticipates an analogous shift for lawyers and tax professionals over coming years, while later clarifying that crossing 51% itself is irrelevant; this is not evidence of a measured legal-work displacement threshold.
qs: We have an OKR in our organization that more than 50% of the pull requests that go into our codebase get written by AI.
And I would say some teams are north of 80% at this point.
Your role now as an engineer is less about writing lines of code and it’s more about building systems around how code gets written.
And I think it will likely take shape in other industries over the years to come.
And whether 51% happens or not, it’s kind of irrelevant.

kp.k: Delegation shifts lawyers toward governance without transferring accountability
kp.d: In his future outlook, Hron predicts that agents' execution of work and decision-making will shift professionals from doing work toward governing its production. He recommends anticipating the systems needed to trust and stand behind delegated outputs. Although execution becomes more autonomous, he maintains that accountability remains human; this is a governance-oriented forecast, not a claim that autonomous outputs can safely be relied on without professional responsibility.
qs: that means now that I am delegating actual work and decision-making to an AI, delegating actual work product to a non-human.
Your role now changes from doing the work to governing the work.
how do I build the systems that give me the trust to stand behind the work that gets created?
the accountability does not shift away from the human in this process, right?

kp.k: Hands-on AI use builds intuition and expands technical oversight
kp.d: Hron recommends frequent practical use to understand AI capabilities and implications for teams, talent and products. As cross-domain experiential evidence, he says AI lets him inspect code, commits and issues across Thomson Reuters' 140 products and thousands of engineers with greater depth than previously feasible, reducing ramp-up and context-switching obstacles. This is a personal account rather than a controlled assessment of managerial productivity.
qs: Then you come into TR, and we’ve got 140 products and thousands of engineers.
My level of depth in the code itself is far more than it could have ever been otherwise because of the ramp-up time and context switching.
whatever it is, go use it, and use it a lot.
The more you do, the better your intuition becomes for where this is going and what impacts you think it might have on your teams, your talent, on the products you’re building, etc.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hron predicts a shift from lawyers performing work to governing agent-produced work, while arguing that trusted content, verification capabilities and proprietary knowledge remain differentiators as interfaces become more interchangeable.
pts.d: Joel Hron, Thomson Reuters’ CTO, makes several related claims. First, tool-equipped legal agents expand research beyond litigation preparation into routine tasks such as revising contractual provisions. Second, products such as Litigation Document Analyzer speed up human verification by identifying assertions and presenting their support or lack of support. Third, MCP changes how legal capabilities are accessed rather than eliminating the value of those capabilities: specialist agents can operate inside other platforms or in workflows without a dedicated user interface. Fourth, he characterises Anthropic’s standalone legal plugins as basic instructions rather than complete systems for trust and verification, while allowing that they can incorporate CoCounsel tools. Fifth, firms that organise proprietary knowledge effectively for agent use can gain competitive advantage. Finally, he predicts that delegation to agents will shift lawyers’ and tax professionals’ roles toward constructing governance systems, without transferring accountability away from humans. His engineering analogy concerns AI-written code and the resulting shift toward tests, architecture and guidance; it is not evidence that a specified proportion of legal work has already been automated.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Hron’s product-development experience, customer conversations, descriptions of system functionality and internal engineering adoption figures; no comparative legal accuracy or productivity study is supplied.
pts.d: At 05:30, Hron cites approximately 1.9–2 billion Westlaw and Practical Law documents and 1.5 billion KeyCite validity signals as resources supporting the company’s approach. These figures describe available content and signals, not measured accuracy. He reports trust and accountability concerns from recent meetings with corporate customers, Am Law 100 and global large-law firms, and major tax firms. At 10:30, he describes Litigation Document Analyzer’s claim-by-claim support table as the mechanism for faster verification, but gives no measured time savings. At 12:59, he reports observing firms build their own interfaces and use general-purpose AI tools. At 36:16, he describes adapting Westlaw APIs for agents’ different patterns of content consumption. His cross-domain evidence includes an organisational target for more than half of codebase pull requests to be AI-written, with some teams reportedly exceeding 80%, and his personal experience using AI to understand code across teams. These are internal reports and experience-based observations, not independent benchmarks. His claims about plugins, durable market advantage and future professional roles are technical assessments and predictions made from his position as a vendor executive.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Hron distinguishes present product development and adoption from a conditional, multi-year shift in professional work; he does not predict a fixed date or numerical threshold for legal automation.
pts.d: In this source, labelled 2026, Hron describes the next CoCounsel version as currently in beta and describes agent-oriented development and engineering adoption as already occurring. His broader professional-role prediction is framed as likely to spread to other industries over the years to come, with preparation needed now. The 51% figure is explicitly a mental exercise, not a necessary threshold or forecast for lawyers. Faster verification does not imply perfect output: Hron says legal work may never be 100% accurate. His interface prediction is qualified by task: dedicated CoCounsel experiences remain useful when legal work requires substantial verification, whereas other tasks may run through email, Word or general-purpose AI interfaces. His criticism of Anthropic plugins applies to them standing alone; he expressly allows their combination with verification tools. Competitive advantage from institutional knowledge depends on codifying it better than competitors and making it available in agent-native forms. Security and trust are described as constraints on translating AI capability into real-world application.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are practising lawyers, corporate legal users, law firms, legal software providers and their development teams; tax professionals and engineers supply parallel examples.
pts.d: For lawyers conducting research, drafting contracts or preparing litigation documents, Hron anticipates more agent-performed work, broader use of legal research and tooling that assists human verification. Professionals remain accountable for work sent to clients and courts. Law firms and corporations may consume specialist legal capabilities inside general-purpose platforms or their own systems, while their institutional knowledge becomes an important investment priority. Hron’s reported customer evidence particularly concerns corporate users, Am Law 100 and global large-law firms, and major tax firms; it does not establish separate outcomes for solos, small firms or underserved individuals. For legal software providers, his claim shifts emphasis from owning a single interface to delivering trusted capabilities wherever work occurs. Within providers, agent teams develop legal capabilities while interface teams support human interaction, context provision and understanding of output. Engineers already illustrate, in his account, the movement toward governing AI production; lawyers and tax professionals are the proposed next analogues. Thomson Reuters is discussed as a software and content provider, not as an ALSP or law firm; Hron’s law-firm comparison is an analogy about organising knowledge.
